questions.q: What makes a report a matrix report instead of a summary report?
options: Adding a chart to the report
Grouping by columns in addition to rows
questions.explain: A summary report only groups rows. A matrix report adds a second dimension by also grouping columns, turning the report into a true grid.

questions.q: In a matrix report grouped by Owner (rows) and Stage (columns), what does a single cell represent?
options: The grand total of the entire report
The summarized value for records matching that owner AND that stage
The summarized value for that owner only, ignoring stage
questions.explain: Each cell in a matrix report is the intersection of one row group and one column group, so it reflects only the records that match both.

questions.q: Where does a matrix report's grand total appear?
options: It doesn't have one; only row and column subtotals exist
In the bottom-right corner, where the row and column subtotals meet
questions.explain: Row subtotals run along the right edge, column subtotals along the bottom, and the single grand total sits at their intersection in the bottom-right corner.

questions.q: A manager wants to compare pipeline across both sales reps and deal stages on one screen. Which report format fits best?
options: Summary with a single row grouping
Joined, with one block per rep
questions.explain: Comparing one dimension (reps) against another (stages) at the same time is exactly what a matrix report is for — a single grid showing every combination.

questions.q: If you only need one level of grouping, with no need to cross it against a second dimension, which format is simpler and faster to read than a matrix report?
questions.explain: A summary report (rows only) is simpler to build and read when you don't need the second, column-based grouping dimension a matrix report adds.
